Mujahid asked Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, about "dubur al-layl" [the end/back of the night], and he left him until he heard the first caller to the dawn prayer, then said to him: "O Mujahid, this is the time when the night has turned back." Qatada said: "dabara al-layl" means "it turned away." The poet said:

"And my father, who left the kings and their multitude / in a humbled, still [grave], like yesterday that has passed."

And the Arabs say in their speech: "like yesterday, the one that turned away." Abu 'Ali said: Both recitations are good.

﴿Asfara al-ṣubḥ﴾ [the dawn brightened] means: it shone and its light spread well before the sunrise. The brightening (al-isfār) is ordered in stages: a first, a middle, and a last. From this root come al-safr, al-sifr, al-safīr, and "safarat al-mar'a 'an wajhihā" [the woman unveiled her face]. All of these return to the meaning of manifestness and clearing. 'Isa ibn al-Fudayl and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿إذا أسْفَرَ﴾ [idhā asfara], so the meaning is: it cast the darkness off its face. Abu Hatim considered this weak.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest [matters]﴾: Qatada, Abu Razin, and others said the pronoun refers to Hell. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the warning and the matter of the Hereafter, so it is for the situation and the account, and this verse would be like His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: It is a mighty news﴾ [Sad 38:67] ﴿from which you turn away﴾ [Sad 38:68]. And "al-kubar" is the plural of "kabīra." Most of the reciters read ﴿لإحْدى﴾ [la-iḥdā] with a hamza in the alif of "iḥdā." It is reported from Ibn Kathir that he read ﴿حِدى﴾ [ḥidā] without a hamza, and this is the recitation of Nasr ibn 'Asim. Abu 'Ali said: The easing in "la-iḥdā al-kubar" is to make the hamza between-between (bayn bayn, an intermediate sound). As for omitting the hamza, it is not analogical, though it has occurred. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:

"O Abu al-Mughira, many a difficult matter / I relieved it by my denial, and its ... [words]."

And Tha'lab recited:

"If I do not fight, then clothe me in a veil, / and anklets on both hands, four of them."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a warning to mankind﴾: al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: No warner is more severe than the Fire. This statement implies that ﴿nadhīran﴾ [a warning] is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿innahā﴾ [indeed it], or of His saying ﴿la-iḥdā﴾ [one of]. The same also holds, by the probability, if ﴿innahā﴾ is intended to refer to the account of the Hereafter and the situation of the return. Abu Razin said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, is the Warner, and this statement implies that ﴿nadhīran﴾ is governed by a verb whose supposed form is: "Worship a warner for mankind," or "Call upon a warner for mankind." Ibn Zayd said: [He is] Muhammad ﷺ, and this statement implies that ﴿nadhīran﴾ is governed by a verb whose supposed form is: "Announce a warner," or "Convey a warner," and similar. It is also possible that ﴿nadhīran﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So how was My denial?﴾ [al-Mulk 67:18]. This is al-Khalil's choice regarding this verse, mentioned by al-Tha'labi, who said: For this reason it is used as a description of the feminine.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾ [nadhīrun] with a raf' [nominative], by supposing a pronoun "huwa" [he].

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿to whichever of you wills to advance or to lag behind﴾: al-Hasan said: It is a threat, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29]. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿to whichever of you wills to advance or to lag behind﴾: al-Hasan said: It is a threat, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We surely know those of you who go before, and We surely know those who lag behind﴾ [al-Hijr 15:24].

**The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:**

It is an explanation regarding the warning, and an announcement to everyone who takes the path of guidance and truth, if he verifies his reflection; that is: or the one who, by his own heedlessness and poor reflection, lags behind this rank.

Then this meaning was reinforced by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾, since by this statement it is established that the negligent one is held in pledge by his evil deeds. Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is: every soul upon which the word of punishment has been fulfilled. God, Exalted is He, does not hold any of the people of Paradise in pledge, God willing. The ha' in ﴿rahīna﴾ [pledged] is for emphasis, or it is due to the feminine form of the word, not to the meaning of "person."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except the companions of the right﴾ is an exception that is clearly disjoined, and its implied form is: "but the companions of the right." That is because they did not earn what they are pledged for. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: The companions of the right in this verse are the children of the Muslims. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: They are the angels, peace be upon them. Al-Dahhak said: They are those for whom the goodly reward from God has preceded. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: They are the sincere Muslims, and they are not held in pledge.

Then God, Exalted is He, mentioned the state of the companions of the right, that they are in gardens, where some of them ask others about those of their acquaintances who were absent. Then, when they learn that they [the absent ones] are criminals in the Fire, they say to them, or the angels say: ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾. And "salaka" means: caused to enter. From it comes the saying of Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

"Until they threaded the hides of them / in a leather of the offspring of the she-camel of the far horizons, long-haired."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 74, verses 43–56:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed,﴾ ﴿nor did we feed the needy,﴾ ﴿and we used to engage in vain talk along with those who engaged in it,﴾ ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Recompense,﴾ ﴿until there came to us the certainty."﴾ ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them.﴾ ﴿Then what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder,﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion?﴾ ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out.﴾ ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed, it is a Reminder;﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it.﴾ ﴿And they will not remember unless Allah wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾

This is the confession of the disbelievers against themselves. In the denial of prayer is included faith in Allah the Exalted, knowledge of Him, humility before Him, and worship. Prayer encompasses most of the religion, the commands of Allah the Exalted, and the obligations of the creed. Feeding the needy encompasses charity, whether obligatory or voluntary, and every kind of good that the Sharia urges, by word or deed. "Engaging in vain talk along with those who engage in it": its customary meaning is falsehood. Qatada said: the meaning is that whenever a deviator went astray, they went astray with him. Denying the Day of Recompense is manifest disbelief in Allah the Exalted.

"Al-yaqin" (certainty), in my view, means: the truth of what they used to deny, namely the return to Allah the Exalted and the Hereafter. The exegetes said: al-yaqin is death. In my view, this is subsequent here, because death itself is a certainty for the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in this world, so they became certain of it after death. The interpretation of al-yaqin as death occurs only in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

Then Allah the Exalted informed that the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them, so it is established from this that there are interceders. There are hadiths on the correctness of this meaning. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angels will intercede, then the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs, then the righteous will intercede. Then Allah the Exalted will say: 'My servants have interceded, and there remains the intercession of the Most Merciful of the merciful.' So no one will remain in the Fire who had faith." Al-Hasan narrated that Allah the Exalted admits, through the intercession of a man from this nation, a number of people into Paradise equal to the tribes of Rabi'a and Mudar. In the narration of Abu Qilaba: more than the tribe of Banu Tamim. Al-Hasan said: "We used to hear that a martyr intercedes for seventy people of his household."

Then the Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿Then what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder﴾, meaning: and the awaited state is this one described? His saying the Exalted in describing the disbelievers who turn away, in aversion and eagerness in flight: ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ is an affirmation of their ignorance, because donkeys are among the most ignorant of animals. Al-A'mash read "ḥumr" with the mim sukun. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "ḥumrun nafiratun." Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "mustanfaratan" with a fatha on the fa'. The rest read it with a kasra on the fa'. It was differed concerning Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Mujahid. As for the fatha on the fa', its meaning is: he startled them, frightened them from the lion. As for the kasra on the fa', it is based on "nafara" and "istanfara" having one meaning, like "'ajiba" and "ista'jaba" and "sakhira" and "istaskhara," so it is as if they fled themselves. His saying "farrat" strengthens this, and on this basis Abu 'Ali preferred the reading with the kasra.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of "al-qaswarah." Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and 'Ikrima said: al-qaswarah means the archers. Ibn 'Abbas also, Abu Hurayra, and the majority of the lexicographers said: al-qaswarah means the lion. The poet's saying:

Concealed, the brave fear him; as if he were the lion, the tawny lion.

Ibn Jubayr said: "al-qaswarah" means the hunters. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. It was said: "al-qaswarah" means the rumbling of people. It was said: al-qaswarah means the strong men. Labid said:

When we call out a call in our gatherings, there come to us the stubborn, strong men.

Tha'lab said: al-qaswarah means the darkness of the beginning of the night specifically, as opposed to its end. Or the word is derived from "qasr," which is overpowering and subjugation.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out﴾ means: from among these turning-away ones, that is, each person among them wants a book from Allah to be sent down upon him. This was said by 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya and others. It is narrated that some of them said: "If he writes in scrolls what he does, then let him display those scrolls to us," and the verse was revealed. "Munashshara" means: not rolled up, spread out. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "suhufan" with a sukun on the ha', and this is the dialect of Tamima. He read "munshara" with a sukun on the nun and lightening of the shin, and this is on the basis of likening "nashartu al-thawb" to "anshara Allahu al-mayyit," when he revived like the dead. At-Taymi reversed the comparison in his saying:

His good deeds returned his life to him, so it is as if he is, from their spreading, spread out.

One does not say of a dead person who lives "manshur" except by the comparison to a garment. As for the transmitted lexicon, it is (p-468) "nashara al-sahifah" and "anshara Allahu al-mayyit," and it has come from them "nashara Allahu al-mayyit."

His saying the Exalted: "Kalla" is a rejection of their desire, that is: the matter is not so. Then He said the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾. The meaning: this is the cause and reason for their turning away, so their ignorance of the Hereafter was the reason for their refusal of guidance until they perished. Abu Haywa read "takhafuna" with a ta' above, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Amir. Then the Exalted repeated the rejection and rebuke with His saying: "Kalla," and informed that this statement and clarification and this discourse in its entirety is a reminder. Whoever wills, He grants him success in remembering his return. Then He informed that a person's remembrance of his return and his progress toward his salvation is entirely by the will of Allah the Exalted, and nothing happens except by it.

Nafi', the people of Medina, Salam, and Ya'qub read "tudhakkirun" with a ta' above. Abu Ja'far, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Kathir, 'Isa, and al-A'raj read "yadhdhakkarun" with a ya' below. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far with a ta' above and a shadda on the dhal, as if it were "tatadhakkarun," so it was assimilated.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness﴾ is a categorical statement. Its meaning is that Allah the Exalted is worthy by His supreme attributes, His countless blessings, and His irresistible retributions, to be feared and obeyed, and His disobedience and opposition to His command are to be guarded against. And He the Exalted, by His grace and generosity, is worthy to forgive His servants if they fear Him. It is narrated that Anas ibn Malik said the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying, peace be upon him: "Your Lord, may His majesty be exalted, says: 'I am worthy that I be feared, so no partner shall be made with Me. Whoever fears making a god with Me other than Me, I will forgive him.'" Qatada said: He is worthy that His prohibitions be feared, and worthy that He forgive sins.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Muddaththir] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out﴾ means: from among these turning-away ones, that is, each person among them wants a book from Allah to be sent down upon him. This was said by 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya and others. It is narrated that some of them said: "If he writes in scrolls what he does, then let him display those scrolls to us," and the verse was revealed. "Munashshara" means: not rolled up, spread out. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "suhufan" with a sukun on the ha', and this is the dialect of Tamima. He read "munshara" with a sukun on the nun and lightening of the shin, and this is on the basis of likening "nashartu al-thawb" to "anshara Allahu al-mayyit," when he revived like the dead. At-Taymi reversed the comparison in his saying:

His good deeds returned his life to him, so it is as if he is, from their spreading, spread out.

One does not say of a dead person who lives "manshur" except by the comparison to a garment. As for the transmitted lexicon, it is (p-468) "nashara al-sahifah" and "anshara Allahu al-mayyit," and it has come from them "nashara Allahu al-mayyit."

His saying the Exalted: "Kalla" is a rejection of their desire, that is: the matter is not so. Then He said the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾. The meaning: this is the cause and reason for their turning away, so their ignorance of the Hereafter was the reason for their refusal of guidance until they perished. Abu Haywa read "takhafuna" with a ta' above, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Amir. Then the Exalted repeated the rejection and rebuke with His saying: "Kalla," and informed that this statement and clarification and this discourse in its entirety is a reminder. Whoever wills, He grants him success in remembering his return. Then He informed that a person's remembrance of his return and his progress toward his salvation is entirely by the will of Allah the Exalted, and nothing happens except by it.

Nafi', the people of Medina, Salam, and Ya'qub read "tudhakkirun" with a ta' above. Abu Ja'far, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Kathir, 'Isa, and al-A'raj read "yadhdhakkarun" with a ya' below. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far with a ta' above and a shadda on the dhal, as if it were "tatadhakkarun," so it was assimilated.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness﴾ is a categorical statement. Its meaning is that Allah the Exalted is worthy by His supreme attributes, His countless blessings, and His irresistible retributions, to be feared and obeyed, and His disobedience and opposition to His command are to be guarded against. And He the Exalted, by His grace and generosity, is worthy to forgive His servants if they fear Him. It is narrated that Anas ibn Malik said the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying, peace be upon him: "Your Lord, may His majesty be exalted, says: 'I am worthy that I be feared, so no partner shall be made with Me. Whoever fears making a god with Me other than Me, I will forgive him.'" Qatada said: He is worthy that His prohibitions be feared, and worthy that He forgive sins.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Muddaththir] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 74, verses 43–56:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed,﴾ ﴿nor did we feed the needy,﴾ ﴿and we used to engage in vain talk along with those who engaged in it,﴾ ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Recompense,﴾ ﴿until there came to us the certainty."﴾ ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them.﴾ ﴿Then what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder,﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion?﴾ ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out.﴾ ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed, it is a Reminder;﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it.﴾ ﴿And they will not remember unless Allah wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾

This is the confession of the disbelievers against themselves. In the denial of prayer is included faith in Allah the Exalted, knowledge of Him, humility before Him, and worship. Prayer encompasses most of the religion, the commands of Allah the Exalted, and the obligations of the creed. Feeding the needy encompasses charity, whether obligatory or voluntary, and every kind of good that the Sharia urges, by word or deed. "Engaging in vain talk along with those who engage in it": its customary meaning is falsehood. Qatada said: the meaning is that whenever a deviator went astray, they went astray with him. Denying the Day of Recompense is manifest disbelief in Allah the Exalted.

"Al-yaqin" (certainty), in my view, means: the truth of what they used to deny, namely the return to Allah the Exalted and the Hereafter. The exegetes said: al-yaqin is death. In my view, this is subsequent here, because death itself is a certainty for the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in this world, so they became certain of it after death. The interpretation of al-yaqin as death occurs only in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

Then Allah the Exalted informed that the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them, so it is established from this that there are interceders. There are hadiths on the correctness of this meaning. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angels will intercede, then the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs, then the righteous will intercede. Then Allah the Exalted will say: 'My servants have interceded, and there remains the intercession of the Most Merciful of the merciful.' So no one will remain in the Fire who had faith." Al-Hasan narrated that Allah the Exalted admits, through the intercession of a man from this nation, a number of people into Paradise equal to the tribes of Rabi'a and Mudar. In the narration of Abu Qilaba: more than the tribe of Banu Tamim. Al-Hasan said: "We used to hear that a martyr intercedes for seventy people of his household."

Then the Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿Then what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder﴾, meaning: and the awaited state is this one described? His saying the Exalted in describing the disbelievers who turn away, in aversion and eagerness in flight: ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ is an affirmation of their ignorance, because donkeys are among the most ignorant of animals. Al-A'mash read "ḥumr" with the mim sukun. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "ḥumrun nafiratun." Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "mustanfaratan" with a fatha on the fa'. The rest read it with a kasra on the fa'. It was differed concerning Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Mujahid. As for the fatha on the fa', its meaning is: he startled them, frightened them from the lion. As for the kasra on the fa', it is based on "nafara" and "istanfara" having one meaning, like "'ajiba" and "ista'jaba" and "sakhira" and "istaskhara," so it is as if they fled themselves. His saying "farrat" strengthens this, and on this basis Abu 'Ali preferred the reading with the kasra.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of "al-qaswarah." Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and 'Ikrima said: al-qaswarah means the archers. Ibn 'Abbas also, Abu Hurayra, and the majority of the lexicographers said: al-qaswarah means the lion. The poet's saying:

Concealed, the brave fear him; as if he were the lion, the tawny lion.

Ibn Jubayr said: "al-qaswarah" means the hunters. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. It was said: "al-qaswarah" means the rumbling of people. It was said: al-qaswarah means the strong men. Labid said:
